title: Collagen Synthesis — DOMiNANCE Originals
source: KNUST Structural Proteins: Collagen & Elastin lecture (Edwin F. Laing) and study guide

questions.stem: What is the principal mechanical function of collagen in connective tissue?
questions.why: Collagen forms insoluble fibres that provide tensile strength to tissues such as skin and tendon.

questions.stem: Which cell is the major source of collagen and ground substance in connective tissue proper?
questions.why: Fibroblasts synthesize extracellular matrix proteins, including collagen and elastin.

questions.stem: Which transmembrane proteins physically link extracellular matrix proteins to the intracellular cytoskeleton?
questions.why: Integrins span the membrane and connect matrix proteins to cytoskeletal structures.

questions.stem: Which extracellular protein prominently helps cells adhere to the surrounding matrix?
questions.why: Fibronectin is an extracellular adhesive glycoprotein that interacts with cells and other matrix components.

questions.stem: Which collagen type predominates in bone, skin and tendons?
questions.why: Type I is the major fibril-forming collagen of bone, skin, tendons and ligaments.

questions.stem: Which collagen type is especially characteristic of cartilage and vitreous humour?
questions.why: Type II collagen forms fibrils in cartilage and vitreous humour.

questions.stem: Which collagen type is found prominently in blood-vessel walls and reticular connective tissue?
questions.why: Type III collagen contributes to extensible connective tissue, including blood vessels.

questions.stem: Which collagen type forms sheet-like networks in the basal lamina?
questions.why: Type IV is the network-forming collagen associated with basement membranes.

questions.stem: Which collagen type forms anchoring fibrils beneath stratified squamous epithelia?
questions.why: Type VII collagen forms anchoring fibrils that connect basement membrane structures to underlying matrix.

questions.stem: Which collagen type laterally associates with type II fibrils in cartilage?
questions.why: Type IX is a fibril-associated collagen associated with cartilage type II fibrils.

questions.stem: How many alpha polypeptide chains form a tropocollagen triple helix?
questions.why: Tropocollagen comprises three α chains coiled into a long, triple-helical rod.

questions.stem: What proportion of collagen amino acid residues is approximately glycine?
questions.why: The characteristic Gly-X-Y repeat places glycine at nearly every third residue.

questions.stem: Why must glycine occur frequently in the collagen triple helix?

options.label: B
options.text: It is the source of bound vitamin C

options.label: C
options.text: Its small side chain fits the core

questions.why: Only glycine is small enough to fit regularly into the crowded central region of the triple helix.

questions.stem: Which amino acid triplet is commonly repeated in collagen polypeptide chains?
questions.why: Collagen frequently contains the Gly-Pro-Hyp motif, supporting a stable triple-helical structure.

questions.stem: Which modified amino acid particularly contributes to collagen triple-helix thermal stability?
questions.why: Hydroxyproline helps stabilize the triple helix; insufficient hydroxylation weakens its stability at body temperature.

questions.stem: A mutation replaces a glycine normally buried in a collagen helix with a bulky amino acid. What is most directly disrupted?

options.label: A
options.text: Initiation of fatty acid beta oxidation

options.label: B
options.text: Tight packing of the three chains

questions.why: Glycine substitutions disturb the sterically constrained helix and can cause severe type I collagen disorders.

questions.stem: When are proline and lysine residues hydroxylated during collagen biosynthesis?
questions.why: Hydroxylation is a post-translational modification of proline and lysine residues before the stable triple helix assembles.

questions.stem: Which enzyme forms 4-hydroxyproline from selected proline residues of nascent collagen?
questions.why: Prolyl-4-hydroxylase modifies prolyl residues and requires ferrous iron, oxygen, α-ketoglutarate and ascorbate.

questions.stem: Which cofactor maintains the active-site iron of prolyl hydroxylase in its reduced functional state?
questions.why: Ascorbate supports iron-dependent collagen prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases by maintaining active reduced iron.

questions.stem: Which molecule is consumed alongside molecular oxygen during collagen proline hydroxylation?
questions.why: Prolyl hydroxylase is an α-ketoglutarate-dependent dioxygenase, producing succinate and CO₂.

questions.stem: Why does an iron chelator such as alpha-alpha-bipyridyl destabilize newly synthesized collagen?
questions.why: Chelating ferrous iron inhibits the iron-dependent hydroxylases, impairing stable triple-helix formation.

questions.stem: Which enzyme hydroxylates selected lysine side chains of nascent collagen?
questions.why: Lysyl hydroxylase modifies lysine before helix formation; lysyl oxidase acts later in extracellular cross-linking.

questions.stem: Where are glucose and galactose residues attached during collagen processing?

options.label: B
options.text: To the unmodified proline side chains

questions.why: Hydroxylysine residues can be glycosylated by galactosyl- and glucosyltransferases.

questions.stem: Which collagen preparation is expected to show comparatively extensive carbohydrate substitution?
questions.why: The lecture contrasts heavily glycosylated network-forming type IV collagen with the more lightly glycosylated tendon type I.

questions.stem: Why do procollagen terminal propeptides remain attached before secretion?

options.label: A
options.text: They replace the alpha chain backbone

questions.why: Terminal propeptides keep intracellular procollagen soluble and help prevent premature fibril formation.

questions.stem: Where are terminal procollagen propeptides normally removed to permit fibril assembly?
questions.why: Secreted procollagen undergoes extracellular cleavage by procollagen peptidases before fibril assembly.

questions.stem: Which enzyme converts selected lysine residues into reactive allysine for collagen cross-linking?
questions.why: Lysyl oxidase oxidatively deaminates lysine/hydroxylysine residues to aldehydes used in covalent cross-links.

questions.stem: At which stage is the final covalent strengthening of collagen fibrils achieved?
questions.why: Lysyl-oxidase-dependent cross-links between tropocollagen units strengthen assembled extracellular fibrils.

questions.stem: Which metal is particularly important for lysyl oxidase-mediated cross-linking?
questions.why: Lysyl oxidase is a copper-dependent extracellular enzyme.

questions.stem: A patient with poor wound healing and bleeding gums lacks a vitamin needed for collagen hydroxylation. Which condition is likely?
questions.why: Vitamin C deficiency causes scurvy because unstable, poorly hydroxylated collagen weakens connective tissue.

questions.stem: Which collagen biosynthetic step is specifically impaired in nutritional scurvy?
questions.why: Lack of ascorbate reduces prolyl and lysyl hydroxylase activity.

questions.stem: Which clinical combination is characteristic of Ehlers-Danlos syndromes?
questions.why: Ehlers-Danlos syndromes comprise inherited connective-tissue disorders, often causing joint hypermobility, hyperextensible skin and tissue fragility.

questions.stem: A hereditary defect of type I collagen produces brittle bones and repeated fractures. Which disorder fits best?
questions.why: Osteogenesis imperfecta frequently results from type I collagen abnormalities, including glycine substitutions disrupting the helix.

questions.stem: Absence of a procollagen peptidase in cattle produces extremely fragile skin. What is the condition called?
questions.why: Dermatoparaxis in cattle is a procollagen-processing defect that prevents normal collagen fibril assembly.

questions.stem: Which toxin inhibits lysyl oxidase and causes defective collagen cross-linking in lathyrism?
questions.why: Beta-aminopropionitrile from Lathyrus inhibits lysyl oxidase, reducing collagen cross-links.

questions.stem: Which property best distinguishes elastin from collagen in mature tissues?
questions.why: Elastin forms extensible fibres that recoil, while collagen principally provides tensile strength.

questions.stem: Which unusual cross-link is especially characteristic of mature elastin?
questions.why: Desmosine and isodesmosine cross-links are formed from lysine residues in elastin.

questions.stem: How many lysine residues contribute to one desmosine cross-link in elastin?
questions.why: Desmosine is a tetrafunctional cross-link derived from four lysine side chains.

questions.stem: Compared with collagen, mature elastin is notable for relatively little of which residue?
questions.why: Elastin contains glycine and proline but relatively little hydroxyproline compared with collagen.

questions.stem: Which tissue contains abundant elastin because it must expand and recoil with each pulse of blood?
questions.why: The aorta and other large arteries are elastin-rich to accommodate pulsatile pressure.
